Diabetes.name: Diabetes Mellitus
Diabetes.description: Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition characterized by elevated levels of blood glucose over a prolonged period resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.
common_types: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
Prediabetes / Impaired Fasting Glucose
Gestational Diabetes
symptoms: Increased thirst (polydipsia) and frequent urination (polyuria)
Unexplained fatigue and persistent lethargy
Blurred vision and slow wound healing
Frequent infections and peripheral numbness (neuropathy)
Unintended weight loss despite increased appetite
risk_factors: Sedentary lifestyle and low physical activity
Elevated Body Mass Index (BMI >= 25 kg/m2)
Hypertension (BP >= 130/80 mmHg) and dyslipidemia
Family history of Type 2 Diabetes
Age >= 45 years

prefer: Non-starchy fibrous vegetables (spinach, kale, broccoli, bell peppers)
Whole grains with low glycemic index (steel-cut oats, quinoa, barley)
Legumes, lentils, chickpeas, and beans
Lean proteins (tofu, skinless poultry, fish rich in omega-3)
Healthy monounsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, cold-pressed olive oil)
limit: Sugar-sweetened beverages, commercial fruit juices, and sodas
Refined carbohydrates (white flour, polished white rice, pastries)
Deep-fried trans-fat snack foods
Processed meats and high-sodium packaged foods
Excessive simple sugars, desserts, and confectionery

recommended: Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (brisk walking, cycling, swimming) for 150 minutes per week
Resistance training (bodyweight, resistance bands, or light weights) 2 to 3 days per week
Post-meal 10-15 minute gentle walking to blunt postprandial glucose spikes
precautions: Check blood glucose before vigorous exercise if taking insulin or sulfonylureas
Carry fast-acting carbohydrates (glucose tablets or candy) to counter hypoglycemia
Wear supportive, well-fitted footwear to avoid foot ulcers and blisters

lifestyle: Self-monitor fasting blood glucose and postprandial levels regularly
Maintain 7-8 hours of regular, restorative sleep every night
Practice active stress reduction (mindfulness, yoga, diaphragmatic breathing)
Schedule regular HbA1c tests every 3 to 6 months
Undergo annual diabetic retinopathy eye screening and podiatric foot exams
warning_signs: Severe hypoglycemia symptoms: dizziness, sweating, shaking, confusion (< 70 mg/dL)
Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state: extreme thirst, mental confusion, dry mouth (> 300 mg/dL)
Fruity breath odor, nausea, vomiting, or rapid breathing (diabetic ketoacidosis)
Non-healing ulcers, sores, or loss of sensation in the feet or toes
when_to_seek_help: Blood glucose persistently exceeds 250 mg/dL or drops below 54 mg/dL
Sudden blurring of vision or new visual floaters
Signs of systemic infection or open skin sores that do not heal
Persistent chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations

Stroke.name: Cerebrovascular Stroke
Stroke.description: A cerebrovascular stroke occurs when blood flow to a portion of the brain is interrupted or reduced (ischemic), or when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures (hemorrhagic), depriving brain tissue of oxygen and nutrients.
common_types: Ischemic Stroke (Thrombotic or Embolic)
Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA / Warning Mini-Stroke)
Hemorrhagic Stroke (Intracerebral or Subarachnoid)
symptoms: Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg (especially on one side of the body)
Sudden confusion, difficulty speaking, or slurred speech (aphasia/dysarthria)
Sudden difficulty seeing in one or both eyes
Sudden loss of balance, coordination, dizziness, or difficulty walking
Sudden severe headache with no known cause ('thunderclap headache')
risk_factors: Uncontrolled hypertension (primary modifiable risk factor)
Atrial fibrillation, cardiac arrhythmias, or prior heart disease
Diabetes mellitus and metabolic syndrome
Active cigarette smoking and heavy alcohol consumption
Hyperlipidemia (elevated LDL cholesterol and atherosclerosis)
Advanced age, obesity, and carotid artery stenosis

prefer: Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND diet)
Leafy green vegetables and antioxidant-rich berries
Potassium-rich foods (bananas, sweet potatoes, spinach) to support healthy BP
Omega-3 fatty acid sources (flaxseeds, walnuts, chia seeds, fatty fish)
High-fiber whole grains and legumes
limit: High-sodium processed meals, canned soups, and salty seasonings (< 1,500 mg sodium/day)
Saturated animal fats, palm oils, and trans fats
Excessive alcohol intake and energy drinks
Ultra-processed packaged foods with artificial preservatives

recommended: 30 minutes of low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, stationary cycling) 5 days per week
Balance, core stability, and neuromotor training (Tai Chi, light stretching)
Supervised physical and occupational therapy regimens for post-stroke rehabilitation
precautions: Avoid high-intensity isometric straining or heavy weightlifting that spikes blood pressure
Monitor blood pressure before and after physical exertion
Stop immediately if lightheadedness, dizziness, or unsteadiness occurs

lifestyle: Strict adherence to antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and antihypertensive medications
Complete cessation of tobacco and nicotine products
Regular monitoring of blood pressure morning and evening
Screening for and managing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)
Learn and educate family on the 'BE FAST' stroke identification protocol
warning_signs: BE FAST: Balance loss, Eyesight change, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech slurring, Time to call emergency
Transient neurological deficits lasting minutes that spontaneously resolve (TIA)
Sudden explosive occipital headache with neck stiffness
when_to_seek_help: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (911 / 108 / 112) IMMEDIATELY upon any single stroke symptom
Do not wait to see if symptoms improve; intravenous thrombolysis (tPA) has a strict 3 to 4.5-hour therapeutic window

Heart_Disease.name: Heart Failure & Cardiac Risk
Heart_Disease.description: Heart failure is a progressive clinical syndrome where the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to meet metabolic demands (reduced ejection fraction) or requires elevated filling pressures (preserved ejection fraction), driven by myocardial infarction, coronary disease, or chronic hypertension.
common_types: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF / Systolic)
Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF / Diastolic)
Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) / Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)
symptoms: Shortness of breath (dyspnea) on exertion or when lying flat (orthopnea)
Waking up gasping for air at night (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea)
Persistent swelling (edema) in ankles, legs, or abdomen (ascites)
Chronic fatigue, exercise intolerance, and lightheadedness
Persistent cough with pink-tinged or white frothy sputum
risk_factors: Prior myocardial infarction or ischemic heart disease
Chronic systemic hypertension (elevated afterload)
Elevated serum creatinine and cardiorenal syndrome
Diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia (high LDL / low HDL)
Valvular heart disease and cardiomyopathy

prefer: Cardioprotective DASH or Mediterranean dietary pattern
Strict sodium restriction (< 2,000 mg/day, or as prescribed)
Fresh fruits, vegetables, and potassium-balanced whole foods
Plant-based proteins and lean white meat
High-fiber oats and psyllium husk to lower circulating LDL
limit: Table salt, soy sauce, processed cheeses, and cured meats
Fluid intake over prescribed daily limit (often 1.5 - 2 liters/day in decompensated HF)
Full-fat dairy, lard, butter, and deep-fried foods
Caffeinated energy stimulants and excessive alcohol

recommended: Low-resistance interval training with gentle warm-up and cool-down periods
Breathing exercises to optimize ventilatory efficiency
precautions: Avoid exercising during acute decompensation, fever, or fluid overload exacerbation
Do not engage in heavy bench-pressing or valsalva breath-holding maneuvers
Track perceived exertion (Borg scale 11-13 / 'fairly light' to 'somewhat hard')

lifestyle: Daily morning weight monitoring after urination (report gain > 2-3 lbs in 24 hrs or 5 lbs in a week)
Strict compliance with guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT: beta-blockers, ACEi/ARNI, SGLT2i, MRAs)
Elevation of legs when resting to diminish dependent peripheral edema
Annual influenza and pneumococcal immunizations
warning_signs: Sudden rapid weight gain (fluid retention) over 48 hours
Increasing shortness of breath requiring extra pillows to sleep (orthopnea)
Chest tightness, pressure, or radiating pain to jaw, arm, or back
Profound dizziness, presyncope, or sudden loss of consciousness
when_to_seek_help: Resting chest pain or acute severe shortness of breath — seek immediate emergency care
New or worsening lower-extremity edema and sudden weight gain — contact cardiologist within 24 hours

Chronic_Kidney_Disease.name: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
Chronic_Kidney_Disease.description: Chronic Kidney Disease is characterized by gradual, progressive loss of renal excretory and endocrine function over months or years, defined by eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2 or persistent markers of kidney damage (proteinuria/albuminuria).
common_types: Stage 1: Kidney damage with normal eGFR (>= 90)
Stage 2: Mild loss of kidney function (eGFR 60-89)
Stage 3a/3b: Moderate loss of kidney function (eGFR 30-59)
Stage 4: Severe reduction in kidney function (eGFR 15-29)
Stage 5: End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD / eGFR < 15)
symptoms: Swelling around the eyes (periorbital puffiness) and swelling in ankles/feet
Changes in urination frequency (nocturia or decreased urine output)
Persistent fatigue, weakness, and pallor (secondary to renal anemia)
Pruritus (generalized itchy skin) and metallic taste in mouth
Nausea, loss of appetite, and muscle cramping
risk_factors: Diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy is leading cause)
Uncontrolled hypertension causing renal arteriolosclerosis
Glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, or recurrent pyelonephritis
Long-term frequent use of nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs like ibuprofen)
Family history of chronic kidney failure

prefer: Kidney-friendly balanced meals tailored to laboratory stages
Controlled moderate protein intake (0.6 - 0.8 g/kg body weight in non-dialysis CKD)
Low-potassium fruits (apples, berries, grapes, pineapple) if serum potassium elevated
Cauliflower, cabbage, and bell peppers (low in potassium and phosphorus)
Fresh home-cooked meals seasoned with herbs instead of salt
limit: Excessive sodium and table salt (< 2,000 mg/day to control hypertension)
High-potassium foods (bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, oranges) if hyperkalemic
High-phosphorus foods (dairy products, dark colas, processed meats with phosphate additives)
Red meats and excess dietary protein that increases glomerular filtration pressure

recommended: Low-impact regular aerobic activity (walking, stationary cycling, light water aerobics)
Gentle mobility and flexibility exercises to prevent muscle cramps
Moderate endurance exercise 20-30 minutes, 3 to 5 times per week
precautions: Avoid dehydration: replenish fluids in accordance with physician-specified fluid allowance
Avoid contact sports if polycystic kidneys or peritoneal dialysis catheter present
Do not exercise if severely hypertensive (> 180/110) or symptomatic from anemia

lifestyle: Strict blood pressure management (target < 120-130 mmHg systolic per KDIGO)
Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) which induce acute renal injury
Periodic monitoring of serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), eGFR, and urine ACR
Address metabolic bone disease and screen for secondary hyperparathyroidism
warning_signs: Uremic symptoms: intractable nausea, vomiting, mental confusion, or uremic frost
Hyperkalemia: muscle weakness, tingling sensations, or irregular heartbeats
Severe fluid overload: pulmonary crackles, shortness of breath, sudden facial edema
Gross hematuria (cola-colored urine) or complete cessation of urination (anuria)
when_to_seek_help: Inability to pass urine, acute respiratory distress, or severe chest pain — emergency hospital visit
eGFR drops below 30 or serum creatinine rises rapidly — urgent nephrology evaluation

Maternal_Health_Risk.name: Hypertension & Maternal Vascular Risk
Maternal_Health_Risk.description: Hypertension and Maternal Vascular Risk encompasses gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and maternal vascular disorders characterized by elevated systemic vascular resistance, microvascular endothelial dysfunction, and end-organ perfusion risk.
common_types: Gestational Hypertension (BP >= 140/90 after 20 weeks gestation)
Preeclampsia (Hypertension with Proteinuria or End-Organ Impairment)
Severe Preeclampsia / Eclampsia Risk
Chronic Essential Hypertension with Secondary Vascular Risk
symptoms: Persistent high blood pressure (systolic >= 140 mmHg or diastolic >= 90 mmHg)
Severe, persistent frontal or occipital headaches unresponsive to acetaminophen
Visual disturbances (blurriness, flashing lights, scotoma, light sensitivity)
Upper right quadrant abdominal pain or epigastric discomfort
Sudden, pronounced edema of the hands, face, or ankles
risk_factors: Nulliparity (first pregnancy) or history of preeclampsia in previous gestation
Pre-existing chronic hypertension, diabetes, or renal disease
Advanced maternal age (>= 35 years) or adolescent pregnancy
High body mass index (BMI >= 30 kg/m2)
Multiple gestation (twins, triplets) or vascular autoimmune disorders

prefer: Nutrient-dense maternal dietary plan rich in elemental calcium (1,000 - 1,500 mg/day)
Magnesium and folate-rich leafy greens, legumes, and fortified whole grains
Lean proteins and iron-rich foods to prevent concurrent maternal anemia
Adequate hydration with clean water (8-10 glasses daily)
Potassium-rich fruits to modulate vascular tone naturally
limit: Excessive sodium and processed savory foods
High glycemic index refined sugars that provoke gestational glucose spikes
Energy drinks, excessive caffeine (> 200 mg/day), and unpasteurized items
Trans fats and deep-fried heavy meals that impair vascular endothelium

recommended: Gentle prenatal walking 20-30 minutes per day at a comfortable conversational pace
Prenatal yoga, pelvic tilts, and modified stretching routines
Water-supported aquatic exercise to alleviate joint pressure and reduce lower limb edema
precautions: Strictly avoid hot yoga, vigorous interval training, or activities with fall risk
Avoid exercising in the supine position (flat on back) after the first trimester
Cease physical activity immediately if dizziness, contractions, or headache occurs

lifestyle: Frequent prenatal blood pressure monitoring at home and at all scheduled antenatal visits
Low-dose aspirin prophylaxis (81-150 mg/day) starting early second trimester if high risk (per ACOG)
Rest on the left lateral side to optimize uteroplacental and renal blood flow
Regular dipstick or quantitative protein-to-creatinine ratio urine testing
warning_signs: Severe persistent headache, vision changes, or flashing blind spots
Severe right upper quadrant pain under the ribs (liver capsule distension)
Blood pressure >= 160/110 mmHg (severe range hypertension requiring urgent antihypertensives)
Shortness of breath, chest pressure, vaginal bleeding, or decreased fetal movement
when_to_seek_help: Systolic BP >= 160 or Diastolic BP >= 110: Seek IMMEDIATE obstetric emergency care
Headache with visual changes or epigastric pain: Go to the nearest labor and delivery triage

Anemia.name: Clinical Anemia
Anemia.description: Clinical Anemia is a hematological disorder defined by a reduction in total circulating red blood cell mass or hemoglobin concentration, impairing systemic oxygen-carrying capacity to vital organs.
common_types: Iron Deficiency Anemia (Microcytic, Hypochromic — most prevalent)
Vitamin B12 / Folate Deficiency Anemia (Macrocytic / Megaloblastic)
Anemia of Chronic Disease / Renal Anemia (Normocytic)
Hemolytic Anemias and Hemoglobinopathies (Thalassemia, Sickle Cell)
symptoms: Generalized fatigue, weakness, and low stamina
Pale or sallow skin, pale conjunctiva (inner eyelids), and pale nail beds
Shortness of breath and rapid heart rate (tachycardia) during minor exertion
Dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint upon standing (orthostasis)
Cold hands and feet, brittle nails (koilonychia), or restless legs syndrome
risk_factors: Inadequate dietary intake of bioavailable iron, vitamin B12, or folate
Chronic blood loss (heavy menstrual bleeding, gastrointestinal ulcers, hemorrhoids)
Pregnancy and lactation (increased fetal and maternal iron demand)
Malabsorption syndromes (celiac disease, Crohn's, prior bariatric surgery)
Chronic kidney disease or systemic inflammatory disorders

prefer: Heme-iron sources with high bioavailability: lean red meats, poultry, and fish
Non-heme iron foods: lentils, spinach, chickpeas, tofu, pumpkin seeds, and fortified cereals
Vitamin C-rich fruits (oranges, strawberries, tomatoes) consumed alongside iron to boost absorption
Folate and Vitamin B12 rich eggs, fortified nutritional yeast, and green vegetables
Dates, blackstrap molasses, and raisins
limit: Coffee, black tea, and green tea during or within 1 hour of meals (tannins inhibit iron uptake)
High-calcium supplements or antacids taken simultaneously with iron-rich foods
Excessive dietary phytates and unprocessed raw bran that bind minerals
Alcohol consumption which impairs hematopoiesis and folate absorption

recommended: Gentle, low-intensity aerobic conditioning (short leisurely walks, gentle cycling)
Frequent rest breaks between daily activities to conserve metabolic energy
Gradual progressive increase in exercise duration as hemoglobin levels normalize
precautions: Avoid high-intensity strenuous workouts until hemoglobin levels reach safe thresholds (> 10-11 g/dL)
Stop immediately if experiencing chest pain, racing pulse, severe breathlessness, or syncope
Stay well-hydrated to support effective circulating blood volume

lifestyle: Take prescribed oral iron supplements on an empty stomach with a glass of orange juice
Avoid consuming milk, antacids, or calcium tablets within 2 hours of oral iron doses
Undergo repeat complete blood count (CBC) and serum ferritin testing every 6 to 12 weeks
Investigate and identify underlying sources of chronic occult gastrointestinal bleeding
warning_signs: Severe hemoglobin drop below 7.0 g/dL (transfusion threshold in symptomatic patients)
Chest pain (angina pectoris), irregular heart rhythm, or severe shortness of breath at rest
Black tarry stools (melena) or vomiting blood indicating active gastrointestinal bleeding
Syncope (fainting), profound confusion, or extreme cyanosis/pallor
when_to_seek_help: Hemoglobin < 7 g/dL, resting chest pain, or fainting: Seek immediate emergency room evaluation
Persistent fatigue and hemoglobin 7 to 9.5 g/dL: Consult primary physician or hematologist promptly
